item.title: A Zero‐Inflated Geographically Weighted Regression Framework for Spatially Explicit Carbon Emission Proxy Mapping Using OpenStreetMap and Remote Sensing Data Fusion
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Spatially explicit carbon emission proxy mapping at sub‐kilometer resolution requires data sources that capture both physical surface characteristics and functional land use attributes. This study proposes a Zero‐Inflated Geographically Weighted Regression (ZI‐GWR) framework that fuses volunteered geographic information (VGI) from OpenStreetMap with remote sensing data, including VIIRS night‐time lights, Sentinel‐2 indices, Landsat 8 land surface temperature, and ESA WorldCover, aggregated to a 500 × 500 m grid across Berlin and Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany. A five‐model comparison (OLS, SLM, SEM, GWR, ZI‐GWR) demonstrates that ZI‐GWR achieves the lowest residual spatial autocorrelation and systematic bias in peri‐urban contexts; in Berlin where structural zeros are rare (3.0%), GWR outperforms ZI‐GWR on goodness of fit, a result consistent with zero‐inflation theory. Feature ablation confirms that VGI alone outperforms remote sensing alone (R2 = 0.909 vs. 0.633 in Berlin), establishing the necessity of data fusion. Partial correlation analysis confirms that 68%–71% of validation correlation in Berlin is independent of the shared night‐time light component, and external validation against the EDGAR v8.0 inventory yields Spearman ρ=0.756$$ \rho =0.756 $$ (p<0.001$$ p<0.001 $$). Temporal change detection reveals divergent emission proxy trajectories between 2022 and 2024, with Berlin increasing and Brandenburg declining, highlighting spatially heterogeneous dynamics undetectable from national inventories.

ABSTRACT

Spatially explicit carbon emission proxy mapping at sub-kilometer resolution requires data sources that capture both physical surface characteristics and functional land use attributes. This study proposes a Zero-Inflated Geographically Weighted Regression (ZI-GWR) framework that fuses volunteered geographic information (VGI) from OpenStreetMap with remote sensing data, including VIIRS night-time lights, Sentinel-2 indices, Landsat 8 land surface temperature, and ESA WorldCover, aggregated to a 500 × 500 m grid across Berlin and Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany. A five-model comparison (OLS, SLM, SEM, GWR, ZI-GWR) demonstrates that ZI-GWR achieves the lowest residual spatial autocorrelation and systematic bias in peri-urban contexts; in Berlin where structural zeros are rare (3.0%), GWR outperforms ZI-GWR on goodness of fit, a result consistent with zero-inflation theory. Feature ablation confirms that VGI alone outperforms remote sensing alone (R 2 = 0.909 vs. 0.633 in Berlin), establishing the necessity of data fusion. Partial correlation analysis confirms that 68%–71% of validation correlation in Berlin is independent of the shared night-time light component, and external validation against the EDGAR v8.0 inventory yields Spearman ρ=0.756$$ \rho =0.756 $$ (p<0.001$$ p<0.001 $$). Temporal change detection reveals divergent emission proxy trajectories between 2022 and 2024, with Berlin increasing and Brandenburg declining, highlighting spatially heterogeneous dynamics undetectable from national inventories.

item.title: Evaluating DEM‐Derived Hydrological Priors for U‐Net‐Based Sentinel‐1 SAR Flood Segmentation
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Floods are among the most destructive natural hazards. Rapid and accurate flood extent mapping is essential for disaster response, risk assessment, and post‐disaster management. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery provides all‐weather and day‐and‐night observation capabilities and has become an important data source for flood monitoring. However, SAR backscatter alone does not explicitly represent terrain and drainage conditions. To examine whether complementary terrain information benefits flood mapping, this study systematically evaluates the effects of Digital Elevation Model (DEM)‐derived terrain and hydrological priors on SAR flood segmentation. Using the Sen1Floods11 dataset, this study constructs a three‐channel SAR baseline comprising normalized VV and VH polarizations and their pixel‐wise mean. Elevation and hydrological features derived from the GLO‐30 DEM, including flow accumulation (Flow), Topographic Wetness Index (TWI), and Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND), are integrated as additional input channels. To ensure a fair comparison of different input features, the same U‐Net architecture, data split, and training settings are adopted to compare nine input configurations. Cross‐region generalization is further examined using a leave‐one‐region‐out (LORO) evaluation, and an additional DeepLabV3+ experiment is conducted to assess whether the contribution of Flow extends beyond U‐Net. Among the evaluated configurations, SAR+Flow achieved the highest mean IoU, increasing from 0.6800 for the SAR baseline to 0.6879. F1‐score increased from 0.8095 to 0.8151, and recall increased from 0.7958 to 0.8112. Under the LORO setting, SAR+Flow increased the region‐balanced mean IoU from 0.5680 to 0.5797, although improvements occurred in only 4 of the 10 held‐out regions. The DeepLabV3+ comparison also showed a small numerical improvement in mean IoU, increasing from 0.6555 to 0.6595 with the incorporation of Flow. Overall, the results suggest that Flow can provide useful complementary spatial information for SAR flood segmentation, but its contribution varies across geographic regions and model architectures.
